\title{DANG: Adapting Frozen DINOv3 Features with a Token-Pyramid Decoder for Generalizable Polyp Segmentation}
\author{\uppercase{Dang Thanh Tuan}\authorrefmark{1}
AND \uppercase{Le Phu-Nguyen}\authorrefmark{2}}

\address[1]{Department of Artificial Intelligence, FPT University, Ho Chi Minh City 71300, Vietnam (e-mail: tuandtse196418@fpt.edu.vn)}
\address[2]{Faculty of Engineering and Technology, Nguyen Tat Thanh University, Ho Chi Minh City 71300, Vietnam (e-mail: nguyenlp@vaa.edu.vn)}

\markboth
{Dang and Le: DANG: Adapting Frozen DINOv3 Features for Generalizable Polyp Segmentation}
{Dang and Le: DANG: Adapting Frozen DINOv3 Features for Generalizable Polyp Segmentation}

\corresp{Corresponding author: Le Phu-Nguyen (e-mail: nguyenlp@vaa.edu.vn).}

\begin{abstract}
Polyp segmentation networks trained on two colonoscopy centres lose accuracy on frames from other centres and devices. We present DANG, which adapts a frozen DINOv3 ViT-S/16 encoder with convolutional bottleneck adapters, decodes a four-scale token pyramid with a scale-aware decoder, and adds a dual-prototype margin head; only $1.9$M of its $23.5$M parameters are trained. We train on the standard $1{,}450$-image Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB split, develop on the five standard test sets and $1{,}399$ deduplicated PolypGen frames, and hold out $1{,}376$ PolypDB frames as a final test evaluated once. PraNet, Polyp-PVT, PraNet-V2 and SegDINO are retrained from their official code with their own recipes, and every model is scored at its final epoch by one evaluator over five seeds. On the held-out PolypDB, DANG reaches $89.8\%$ mean Dice against $86.7\%$ for the strongest retrained model, Polyp-PVT (paired $p=0.005$). On the development cohorts it gains $7.3$ and $2.7$ points on ETIS-LaribPolypDB and PolypGen and shows no significant difference on CVC-ColonDB; it trails Polyp-PVT by $3.2$ points on the in-domain CVC-ClinicDB and in boundary F1 on three of four external cohorts, and its advantage comes mainly from fewer failed frames. Ablations attribute $5.5$--$10.8$ points on the primary cohorts to the adapters and $0.2$--$1.0$ points, not significant across seeds, to the prototype head. With FP16 weights and CUDA graphs a frame takes $9.3$~ms on an NVIDIA T4.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keywords}
Colonoscopy, deep learning, domain generalization, foundation models, medical image segmentation, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, polyp segmentation, prototype learning.
\end{keywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}
\PARstart{C}{olorectal} cancer is the third most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer death worldwide~\cite{sung2021globocan}, and removing adenomatous polyps during colonoscopy lowers colorectal-cancer mortality~\cite{zauber2012polypectomy}. Pixel-level polyp segmentation supports this by delineating lesion margins. The standard benchmark trains on $1{,}450$ frames from two centres, Kvasir-SEG~\cite{jha2020kvasir} and CVC-ClinicDB, and tests on five public sets~\cite{fan2020pranet}. On the two in-domain test sets current CNN and transformer models exceed $90\%$ mean Dice; on CVC-ColonDB~\cite{tajbakhsh2015automated} and ETIS-LaribPolypDB~\cite{silva2014toward}, which come from other centres and cameras, these models lose $10$--$25$ points (Table~\ref{tab:main}). Generalization to unseen centres, not in-domain accuracy, is the open problem.

Vision foundation models such as DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024dinov2} and DINOv3~\cite{simeoni2025dinov3} are trained on very large image collections and transfer across domains, which makes them natural encoders for this problem. Keeping such an encoder frozen also keeps training cheap and the trainable part small. SegDINO~\cite{yang2025segdino} pairs a frozen DINOv3 with a light decoder; under our protocol, however, it reaches only $43.3\%$ mean Dice on ETIS (Table~\ref{tab:main}). A frozen encoder trained on natural images does not see colonoscopy frames, and its $16$-pixel patch grid is coarser than lesion boundaries, so how the frozen features are adapted and decoded decides whether a frozen foundation model helps.

  \label{fig:arch}

We present \textbf{DANG} (Figure~\ref{fig:arch}) and make three contributions:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{An adapted frozen-foundation-model segmenter.} DANG adapts a frozen DINOv3 ViT-S/16 with convolutional bottleneck adapters, decodes a token pyramid with the scale-aware decoder of the extended SegDINO~\cite{yang2026segdino}, and adds a dual-prototype margin head with test-time self-support. It trains $1.9$M of its $23.5$M parameters and needs no convolutional backbone.
  \item \textbf{A controlled benchmark.} The standard training split; the five standard test sets kept as published; two deduplicated multi-centre cohorts, PolypGen~\cite{ali2023polypgen} and PolypDB~\cite{jha2024polypdb}, the latter held out and evaluated once as a final test; four published models retrained from their official code with their own recipes; final-epoch checkpoints, one evaluator, five seeds, paired tests with multiplicity correction, and boundary and failure-rate metrics next to Dice.
  \item \textbf{Ablations.} Over five seeds we remove the adapters and the prototype head in turn, and on the same frozen encoder and token pyramid we compare three decoders and report what each costs in latency on an NVIDIA T4.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\paragraph{Polyp segmentation.} Architectures progressed from U-Net~\cite{ronneberger2015unet} and UNet++~\cite{zhou2018unetplusplus} to reverse-attention networks: PraNet~\cite{fan2020pranet} mines boundary cues with parallel partial decoders and reverse attention, and CaraNet~\cite{lou2022caranet} adds axial context for small objects. Transformer encoders improved multi-centre generalization in Polyp-PVT~\cite{dong2021polyp} and TransFuse~\cite{zhang2021transfuse}, and EMCAD~\cite{rahman2024emcad} pairs a PVTv2 encoder with an efficient multi-scale convolutional attention decoder. Recent models refine the decoder further: PraNet-V2~\cite{hu2026pranetv2} supervises the background explicitly inside reverse attention, ASGNet~\cite{sun2026asgnet} guides ResNet or PVTv2 features with an adaptive spectral filter, and CSG-Mamba~\cite{wang2026csgmamba} adds convolutional gating to a vision state-space U-Net. Their reported gains are hard to compare: an audit of $27$ polyp segmentation papers~\cite{urooj2026metrics} found at least five incompatible train/test splits of the same datasets, and $26$ of the papers reported no significance test. Label-efficient work on polyps has mostly been semi-supervised; FPGM~\cite{xi2025fpgm}, for example, uses a frequency prior on polyp edges to augment unlabelled images and improve generalization to new centres.

\paragraph{Foundation models for polyps.} SAM applied without prompts segments polyps poorly~\cite{zhou2023samPolyps}, and MedSAM~\cite{ma2024medsam} fine-tunes SAM on a large medical corpus but requires box prompts. SAM~3 is being adapted in the same way: Medical SAM3~\cite{jiang2026medsam3} fully fine-tunes it on $33$ medical datasets, SAM3-Adapter~\cite{chen2025sam3adapter} trains lightweight adapters, and HAT-SAM3~\cite{li2026hatsam3} adapts it to colonoscopy with a highlight-aware boundary regulariser. SAM-Mamba~\cite{dutta2024sammamba} and SAM-MaGuP~\cite{dutta2025sammagup} adapt SAM with Mamba-based priors for zero-shot polyp generalization, at about $103$M parameters and $423$~GFLOPs~\cite{agnihotri2026litebound}. A second line distils foundation models into small networks: Polyp-DiFoM~\cite{agnihotri2025difom}, LiteBounD~\cite{agnihotri2026litebound} and Lite-$\pi$~\cite{agnihotri2026litepi}. Closest to DANG, SegDINO~\cite{yang2025segdino} keeps a DINOv3 encoder~\cite{simeoni2025dinov3} frozen and decodes multi-depth tokens with a light head, and its extended version~\cite{yang2026segdino} arranges the tokens into a multi-scale pyramid with a scale-aware decoder. DANG builds on this pyramid and decoder, adds trained adapters and a prototype margin head, and keeps the foundation model at inference without distillation.

\paragraph{Prototype-based segmentation.} Few-shot semantic segmentation classifies query pixels by their similarity to class prototypes computed from support images~\cite{wang2019panet}. Self-support prototypes~\cite{fan2022ssp} are built from confident features of the query image itself, which narrows the gap between support and query appearance. DANG adopts this self-support idea inside a fully supervised segmenter: learned prototypes and ground-truth anchors give a prior, and image-specific self-support centroids adapt it at test time.

\paragraph{Adapting frozen vision transformers.} Low-rank adaptation (LoRA~\cite{hu2022lora}) adapts frozen transformers with few parameters; Conv-LoRA~\cite{zhong2024convlora} adds convolutional experts to the low-rank branch of SAM's encoder, and convolutional bypass adapters such as Convpass~\cite{jie2022convpass} add a small convolutional residual path to each block. Dense-prediction heads such as DPT~\cite{ranftl2021vision} reassemble ViT tokens from several depths into a multi-scale map. DANG uses a residual convolutional bottleneck after every block of the frozen encoder, in the spirit of these adapters, and a fixed depth-to-stride assignment instead of learned reassembly.

\section{Method}
DANG maps an RGB frame $I\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times352\times352}$ to a polyp probability map $\hat Y=\sigma(Z)$ (Figure~\ref{fig:arch}); Figure~\ref{fig:modules} details its trained components. We write $X^{\uparrow n}$ for bilinear resizing of a map $X$ to $n\times n$ and $s_k$ for stride $k$ relative to the $352\times352$ input.

\begin{figure*}[!t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{../figs/arch_modules.pdf}
  \caption{\textbf{The three trained components of DANG.} \textbf{(a)}~The convolutional bottleneck adapter after each frozen ViT block (Eq.~\eqref{eq:convlora}): a rank-$16$ bottleneck with a depthwise $3\times3$ convolution on the $28\times28$ patch-token grid, whose up-projection starts at zero. \textbf{(b)}~The token pyramid (left column, Eq.~\eqref{eq:pyramid}; levels at $11^2$, $22^2$, $44^2$ and $88^2$) and the scale-aware decoder (Eqs.~\eqref{eq:rdb} and~\eqref{eq:topdown}): each level is refined by a residual depthwise block $R$, fused top-down with the upsampled coarser level and refined again by $R'$; auxiliary $1\times1$ heads give the deep-supervision logits $A_{32},A_{16},A_8$. \textbf{(c)}~The dual-prototype margin head (Eqs.~\eqref{eq:proto_prior} and~\eqref{eq:proto_total}): unit embeddings are scored against learned prototypes and ground-truth anchors, which are updated from the mask during training only, and the resulting prior is refined by image-specific self-support centroids.}
  \label{fig:modules}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Frozen Encoder With Convolutional Adapters}
\label{sec:encoder}
The encoder is DINOv3 ViT-S/16~\cite{simeoni2025dinov3}, kept frozen. The benchmark gives every model $352\times352$ frames; DANG resizes them to $448\times448$ inside the network so that the $16$-pixel patches form a $28\times28$ grid of $384$-dimensional tokens. Each of the $12$ blocks is followed by a residual convolutional bottleneck adapter of rank $r=16$, in the spirit of Conv-LoRA~\cite{zhong2024convlora} and Convpass~\cite{jie2022convpass}, that acts on the patch tokens $x$ of the block output:
\begin{equation}
  x \leftarrow x + W_{\uparrow}\,\mathrm{GELU}\bigl(z+\mathcal{K}_{3\times3}(z)\bigr),\qquad z=W_{\downarrow}x,
  \label{eq:convlora}
\end{equation}
where $W_{\downarrow}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times384}$ and $W_{\uparrow}\in\mathbb{R}^{384\times r}$ are trained, $W_{\uparrow}$ is initialised to zero so that training starts from the frozen encoder, and $\mathcal{K}_{3\times3}$ is a depthwise convolution on the $28\times28$ token grid. The class and register tokens take the linear path $W_{\uparrow}W_{\downarrow}x$ only. Unlike LoRA, the adapter is a non-linear residual module, so it cannot be merged into the frozen weights; the adapters add $0.15$M parameters. We read the normalised patch tokens after blocks $3$, $6$, $9$ and $12$ and project each with a $1\times1$ convolution, batch normalisation and activation to a map $T_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{192\times28\times28}$, $\ell\in\{3,6,9,12\}$.

\subsection{Token Pyramid and Scale-Aware Decoder}
\label{sec:decoder}
Following the token pyramid of the extended SegDINO~\cite{yang2026segdino}, each depth is assigned to one stride, shallow depths to fine strides:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
  P_4 &= \phi_4\bigl(\mathcal{U}(T_3^{\uparrow44})\bigr), & P_8 &= \phi_8\bigl(T_6^{\uparrow44}\bigr),\\
  P_{16} &= \phi_{16}\bigl(T_9^{\uparrow22}\bigr), & P_{32} &= \phi_{32}\bigl(\mathcal{D}(T_{12}^{\uparrow22})\bigr),
\end{aligned}
  \label{eq:pyramid}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{U}$ is a learned depthwise $2\times$ transposed convolution, $\mathcal{D}$ a depthwise convolution with stride $2$, and $\phi_s$ light convolution blocks (separable $3\times3$ at $s_4$ and $s_8$, $1\times1$ at $s_{16}$ and $s_{32}$). The pyramid has no convolutional backbone: all four levels come from the frozen encoder.

The scale-aware decoder of~\cite{yang2026segdino} refines each level with a residual depthwise block
\begin{equation}
  R(x)=x+\gamma\,\mathrm{GELU}\bigl(\mathrm{GN}(W_{1\times1}\,\mathcal{K}_{3\times3}(x))\bigr),
  \label{eq:rdb}
\end{equation}
with a learned scalar $\gamma$ initialised to zero and group normalisation $\mathrm{GN}$, and then fuses the levels top-down,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
  X_{32}&=R'_{32}\bigl(R_{32}(P_{32})\bigr),\\
  X_k&=R'_k\bigl(X_{2k}^{\uparrow}+R_k(P_k)\bigr),\quad k=16,8,4,
\end{aligned}
  \label{eq:topdown}
\end{equation}
where $R_k$ and $R'_k$ are separate blocks of the form of Eq.~\eqref{eq:rdb}. A $1\times1$ convolution on $X_4$ gives the decoder logit $Z_{\text{SAD}}$ at $s_4$ ($88\times88$). For deep supervision during training, $1\times1$ heads on $X_8$, $X_{16}$ and $X_{32}$ give auxiliary logits $A_8$, $A_{16}$ and $A_{32}$; they are not used at inference.

\subsection{Dual-Prototype Margin Head}
\label{sec:proto}
The head concatenates the three deepest maps $T_6$, $T_9$ and $T_{12}$, projects them with a $3\times3$ convolution block and a $1\times1$ convolution to $128$ channels, and normalises each position to a unit embedding $e_{u,v}$ on the $28\times28$ grid. It compares $e_{u,v}$ with $K=8$ learned foreground prototypes $p_k^+$ and $K=8$ background prototypes $p_k^-$ (unit vectors, orthogonally initialised), and with a foreground anchor $a^+$ and background anchor $a^-$:
\begin{align}
  \pi_{\text{prior}}(u,v) &= \tfrac{\tau}{\beta}\Bigl(\log\textstyle\sum_k e^{\beta\langle e_{u,v},p_k^+\rangle}-\log\textstyle\sum_k e^{\beta\langle e_{u,v},p_k^-\rangle}\Bigr)\nonumber\\
  &\quad + w_{\text{a}}\bigl(\langle e_{u,v},a^+\rangle-\langle e_{u,v},a^-\rangle\bigr)+b.
  \label{eq:proto_prior}
\end{align}
The log-sum-exp with fixed sharpness $\beta$ is a soft maximum over prototypes; the temperature $\tau$, the bias $b$ and the bounded anchor weight $w_{\text{a}}$ are learned. During training only, $a^\pm$ are exponential moving averages of the embeddings at positions where the ground-truth mask, average-pooled to $28\times28$, is mostly foreground or mostly background; they start as the normalised means of the prototypes and are fixed at test time. At training and test time the head then forms image-specific self-support centroids~\cite{fan2022ssp} weighted by the prior's own confidence, $c^+=\mathrm{Norm}(\sum_{u,v}q_{u,v}^2e_{u,v})$ and $c^-=\mathrm{Norm}(\sum_{u,v}(1-q_{u,v})^2e_{u,v})$ with $q=\sigma(\pi_{\text{prior}})$ computed from a stop-gradient copy of the prior and a floor of $10^{-4}$ on both weights, and outputs the margin map
\begin{equation}
  \pi_{\text{proto}}=\pi_{\text{prior}}+w_{\text{ss}}\bigl(\langle e,c^+\rangle-\langle e,c^-\rangle\bigr),
  \label{eq:proto_total}
\end{equation}
with a learned bounded weight $w_{\text{ss}}$. The final logit is
\begin{equation}
  Z=\bigl(Z_{\text{SAD}}+0.2\,\pi_{\text{proto}}^{\uparrow88}\bigr)^{\uparrow352}.
  \label{eq:output}
\end{equation}
The prototype margin thus enters the output as a coarse, token-level prior on top of the decoder logit. Constant values are listed in Appendix~\ref{app:impl}.

\subsection{Training Objective}
\label{sec:loss}
DANG is trained with
\begin{align}
  \mathcal{L} &= \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE+Dice}}^{w}(Z,Y)+0.25\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{Tv}}^{w}(Z,Y)+0.1\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{far}}(Z,Y)\nonumber\\
  &\quad +\tfrac{0.25}{3}\textstyle\sum_{k\in\{8,16,32\}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE+Dice}}^{w}(A_k^{\uparrow352},Y)+0.35\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{proto}}.
  \label{eq:loss}
\end{align}
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE+Dice}}$ is $0.5$ binary cross-entropy plus $0.5$ soft Dice with smoothing $1$. In the terms marked $w$, each image is weighted by $w$, which grows as lesion area shrinks and is normalised to mean $1$ in the batch. The Tversky term $\mathcal{L}_{\text{Tv}}$ (smoothing $1$) penalises false negatives more for small lesions. $\mathcal{L}_{\text{far}}$ is the unweighted mean over all pixels of the predicted probability times the average of four indicators of lying outside the ground truth dilated by $4$, $8$, $14$ and $20$ pixels. $\mathcal{L}_{\text{proto}}$ applies the cross-entropy, Dice and Tversky terms to $\pi_{\text{proto}}$ against the mask average-pooled to $28\times28$. Exact forms are in Appendix~\ref{app:impl}. During training, each image's amplitude spectrum is mixed with that of another image in the batch with probability $0.5$, keeping its phase (Fourier amplitude mix~\cite{xu2021fact}), to vary colour and illumination statistics.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\subsection{Data}
\label{sec:data}
We use the standard split~\cite{fan2020pranet}: $900$ Kvasir-SEG and $550$ CVC-ClinicDB images for training, and the five standard test sets kept exactly as published (Table~\ref{tab:data}). Because these test sets are small, we add two multi-centre cohorts. From PolypGen~\cite{ali2023polypgen} we keep $1{,}399$ of $1{,}536$ frames from its six centres, after dropping $125$ frames with empty masks and $12$ within-set duplicates. From PolypDB~\cite{jha2024polypdb} we keep $1{,}376$ frames of six centre and modality groups (white light, BLI, FICE, LCI and NBI); we drop its Norwegian white-light group, which comes from the hospital that collected Kvasir-SEG. The kept NBI group also comes from Norwegian and Swedish sources and may include that hospital, so for this group only the imaging modality, not necessarily the centre, is new. Every kept frame is compared against all $1{,}450$ training images and the frames already kept from its own set. Two frames count as duplicates when their MD5 hashes match, or when the Pearson correlation of their $32\times32$ grey-scale thumbnails, taken after cropping the dark endoscope border, is at least $0.97$ and their masks overlap with IoU at least $0.8$. A $64$-bit difference hash was tried first and rejected because the black border dominates it on endoscopy frames. The highest thumbnail correlation of a kept frame with any training image is $0.94$ for PolypGen and $0.92$ for PolypDB.

Following the standard protocol, the benchmark has no validation split, and DANG's design was developed while inspecting the test cohorts. We therefore treat CVC-ColonDB, ETIS and PolypGen, the three cohorts that are external to the training centres and large enough for per-image statistics, as primary development cohorts, and PolypDB, which no design decision used, as the confirmatory test. Kvasir and ClinicDB share their training centres, and ClinicDB and CVC-300 are small (one image can move mean Dice by up to $1.6$ and $1.7$ points); we report them for comparability.

\subsection{Models and Training}
\label{sec:training}
DANG is trained for $20$ epochs at $352\times352$ with batch size $16$, AdamW, linear warm-up and cosine decay, gradient clipping, mixed precision and an exponential moving average of the weights; all hyperparameters are listed in Table~\ref{tab:impl}. There is no validation split and no checkpoint selection: we evaluate the moving-average weights after the last epoch.

Published scores rest on incompatible splits and are rarely tested for significance~\cite{urooj2026metrics}, and the released training scripts of some models select checkpoints on test data. We therefore retrain the compared models instead of copying their numbers. PraNet~\cite{fan2020pranet}, Polyp-PVT~\cite{dong2021polyp} and PraNet-V2~\cite{hu2026pranetv2} are retrained from their official code with the training settings of their papers and released scripts, and SegDINO~\cite{yang2025segdino}, which uses the same frozen DINOv3 ViT-S/16 encoder as DANG, with those of its paper. All models are thus evaluated under one protocol but trained with their own recipes, and every model is evaluated at its final epoch. When a seed was run twice, the first completed run is used.

\subsection{Metrics and Statistics}
\label{sec:stats}
All models are scored by one evaluator. Logits are resized bilinearly to the native ground-truth resolution, passed through the sigmoid and thresholded at $0.5$; Dice is computed per image and averaged over the images of a cohort (for PolypGen and PolypDB, over all frames of all centres). For comparison with published tables we also report the toolbox mean Dice, the Dice averaged over $256$ thresholds of the min-max-normalised probability map, which is the metric of the evaluation scripts behind PraNet, Polyp-PVT and PraNet-V2. As secondary metrics we report boundary F1 (contours matched within $2$ pixels), the $95$th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) at $352\times352$, and the failure rate, the share of frames with Dice below $50\%$.

Five seeds ($42$--$46$) are run for every model, and the seed is the unit of inference. At the seed level, a two-sided paired $t$-test compares the per-seed mean Dice of DANG and each compared model over matched seed labels ($n=5$); because runs of different codebases share no randomness, we also report Welch's unpaired test as a sensitivity check. For each compared model, Holm's procedure~\cite{holm1979simple} corrects the seed-level tests over the three primary cohorts; as a second check we apply Holm jointly over all four published models and three cohorts. At the image level, a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test~\cite{wilcoxon1945individual} compares per-image Dice averaged over the five seeds, with zero differences dropped. Frames from the same video are not independent, and the test is conditional on the five trained models, so we use it only descriptively, together with the counts of images on which each model is better; no claim in this paper rests on image-level tests alone. Statistics were computed with SciPy.

Inference cost is measured for all models in one process on one NVIDIA T4 at batch size $1$ and $352\times352$ input ($256\times256$ for SegDINO, its own resolution): the median of $300$ timed device-side forward passes after $50$ warm-up passes on resident input tensors (no data transfer or post-processing), averaged over two passes of the whole benchmark, which differ by at most $0.1$~ms. We time three modes: FP16 autocast (eager), FP16 weights, and FP16 weights replayed from a CUDA graph. We also report multiply-accumulate operations (MACs) per frame and the parameters of the timed model, frozen weights included.

\subsection{Comparison With Retrained Published Models}
\label{sec:sota}
Table~\ref{tab:main} compares DANG with the four retrained models.

\paragraph{Held-out test.} On PolypDB, evaluated once after all design decisions, DANG reaches $89.8\pm0.1\%$: $3.1$ points above Polyp-PVT ($86.7\%$; $95\%$ confidence interval of the seed-level difference $1.5$ to $4.7$ points, paired $p=0.005$, Welch $p=0.005$), $4.4$ and $5.0$ points above PraNet-V2 and PraNet, and $17.4$ points above SegDINO. Averaged over the six PolypDB groups instead of over frames, DANG reaches $88.3\%$ against $84.3\%$ for Polyp-PVT. Most frames are segmented about equally well by the two models: DANG is better on $713$ frames and worse on $662$, and the median per-frame difference is below $0.1$ point, so the higher mean comes mainly from fewer failed frames ($3.8$ against $7.5\%$ of frames below $50\%$ Dice, Table~\ref{tab:secondary}).

\paragraph{Development cohorts.} Among the retrained models, Polyp-PVT is the strongest on ColonDB ($80.9\%$) and PolypGen ($81.4\%$), and PraNet-V2 on ETIS ($75.4\%$). DANG reaches $80.7\%$ on ColonDB, $82.7\%$ on ETIS and $84.2\%$ on PolypGen. On ETIS and PolypGen it is $7.3$ and $2.7$ points above the best retrained model, with the smallest seed-to-seed SD of the compared models on the three primary cohorts ($0.2$--$0.7$ points). On ColonDB its difference to Polyp-PVT, $-0.2$ points ($95\%$ confidence interval $-1.4$ to $+1.1$), is not significant.

\paragraph{In domain and CVC-300.} On Kvasir DANG has the highest mean ($92.2\%$, $1.2$ points above Polyp-PVT), but it is better than Polyp-PVT on only $40$ of the $100$ images; the higher mean comes from a few frames on which Polyp-PVT fails. On ClinicDB it is $3.2$ points below Polyp-PVT and worse on $55$ of the $62$ images, a systematic deficit; a plausible reason, which we did not test, is that the fully fine-tuned encoders of the compared models fit the training centres more closely than a frozen encoder. On CVC-300 its mean is $1.0$ point below PraNet, although it is better on $40$ of the $60$ images.

\paragraph{SegDINO.} SegDINO, which uses the same frozen encoder with a light decoder, stays far below every other model, at $51.5\%$ on ColonDB and $43.3\%$ on ETIS. It is trained at the $256\times256$ input of its paper and without adapters, so this gap mixes input resolution, adaptation and decoder; Section~\ref{sec:components} shows that DANG with a fully frozen encoder still exceeds it by $14.5$--$28.7$ points on the primary cohorts. We keep it as the reference for a frozen foundation model with a light head: DANG uses the same frozen weights and trains a comparable number of parameters ($1.9$M against $2.5$M).

\paragraph{Per centre.} Figure~\ref{fig:centre}a splits PolypGen by centre. DANG has the highest mean Dice on all six centres. Its margin over the best retrained model is $0.5$--$2.3$ points on Paris, Padova, Aviano and Alexandria and $6.1$ and $8.9$ points on Oslo and Oxford, the two centres on which every retrained model stays below $66\%$. On PolypDB (Figure~\ref{fig:centre}b), DANG is the best model on five of the six groups. Its gains are largest on narrow-band imaging ($83.8$ against $75.8\%$ for Polyp-PVT) and blue-light imaging ($81.8$ against $74.3\%$), two of the four virtual-chromoendoscopy modalities absent from training; on the $30$ Swedish white-light frames it is $0.9$ points below Polyp-PVT. These per-group values are five-seed means without per-group tests, and four of the six groups have $70$ frames or fewer. Averaged over centres, PolypGen gives $82.2\%$ for DANG against $78.8\%$ for Polyp-PVT.

\paragraph{Examples.} Figure~\ref{fig:qual} shows six frames drawn at random from the primary cohorts. Five are segmented well by PraNet, PraNet-V2, Polyp-PVT and DANG, while SegDINO adds scattered false positives on several of them (Dice $67$--$89\%$). On the second ETIS frame PraNet finds only a fragment of the lesion (Dice $3\%$), PraNet-V2 adds large false positives on the surrounding folds ($49\%$) and SegDINO reaches $12\%$, while Polyp-PVT and DANG reach $85$ and $86\%$.

\paragraph{Statistical tests.} Table~\ref{tab:stats} gives the tests on the primary cohorts. On ETIS and PolypGen, DANG is better than every retrained model at the seed level after Holm correction; against Polyp-PVT the adjusted $p$-values are $0.007$ and $0.031$. The conclusions are unchanged with Welch's unpaired test ($p=0.001$ and $0.008$ against Polyp-PVT) and with one Holm family over all twelve comparisons with published models (largest adjusted $p$ for these claims $0.031$). Descriptively, DANG is better on $123$ of $196$ ETIS images (worse on $70$) and on $746$ of $1{,}399$ PolypGen frames (worse on $647$). On ColonDB, DANG is better than PraNet, PraNet-V2 and SegDINO and not significantly different from Polyp-PVT (adjusted $p=0.72$; $187$ images better, $191$ worse).

\paragraph{Boundaries and failures.} Table~\ref{tab:secondary} reports secondary metrics on the four external cohorts. DANG has the lowest HD95 and the lowest failure rate on all four; on ETIS, for example, $7.2\%$ of its frames fall below $50\%$ Dice, against $17.2$--$51.9\%$ for the retrained models. Its boundary F1, however, is $1.5$--$3.5$ points below that of Polyp-PVT on ColonDB, PolypGen and PolypDB and higher only on ETIS. DANG's Dice gains therefore come mainly from fewer missed or fragmented lesions rather than from sharper contours; the stride-$16$ token grid of the encoder may limit boundary precision.

Table~\ref{tab:components} removes each trained component of DANG in turn, over five seeds.

\paragraph{Adapters.} Using the DINOv3 encoder fully frozen, without the adapters, costs $7.3$, $10.8$ and $5.5$ points on ColonDB, ETIS and PolypGen, the largest effect in the paper (seed-level adjusted $p<0.001$). The $0.15$M adapter parameters are therefore what lets the frozen encoder transfer to colonoscopy. The fully frozen variant still exceeds SegDINO by $21.9$, $28.7$ and $14.5$ points on these cohorts, so SegDINO's low scores (Table~\ref{tab:main}) are not explained by the missing adapters alone; its lower input resolution and lighter decoder also contribute.

\paragraph{Prototype head.} Removing the dual-prototype margin head, its logit term and its loss lowers Dice by $0.7$, $1.0$ and $0.2$ points on the primary cohorts and halves the trained parameters ($1.94$M to $0.91$M). The effect is small and not significant over five seeds (adjusted $p=0.20$, $0.31$ and $0.31$; the $95\%$ confidence intervals of the differences, $-0.1$ to $1.4$, $-0.6$ to $2.5$ and $-0.1$ to $0.6$ points, include zero); descriptively, DANG is better on $224$ of the $380$ ColonDB images and worse on $154$. On Kvasir, ClinicDB and CVC-300 the differences are $-0.2$, $+0.1$ and $-0.4$ points. We keep the head because its effect points the same way on all three primary cohorts, but the evidence for it is weak.

\subsection{Choice of Decoder}
\label{sec:ablation}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} compares three decoder configurations, each with its own deep supervision, on the same frozen DINOv3 ViT-S/16 with adapters and the same token pyramid, with the same loss family, recipe, evaluator and T4 hardware, over five seeds each. Besides the scale-aware decoder of DANG, we test four top-down stages that predict foreground and background logits gated by boundary uncertainty, with a $768$-channel fusion head and a prototype-anchored spatial support envelope (PASSE) on the output logits, and a query decoder in which one foreground and one background query attend to the pyramid with masked cross-attention.

\paragraph{Accuracy and cost.} Over five seeds the fg/bg decoder with PASSE is the most accurate variant: it is $1.0$, $0.4$ and $0.5$ points above DANG on ColonDB, ETIS and PolypGen. The differences are small and not significant at the seed level after Holm correction (adjusted $p=0.064$, $0.116$ and $0.076$); descriptively, the fg/bg decoder is better on $251$ ColonDB images and worse on $128$. The query decoder lies between the two on ColonDB and PolypGen and below both on ETIS; none of its differences to DANG is significant at the seed level, and descriptively it is better than DANG on $217$ of $380$ ColonDB images and $886$ of $1{,}399$ PolypGen frames. We select the scale-aware decoder for its cost: against the fg/bg decoder with PASSE it removes $1.5$M parameters and $30\%$ of the MACs ($25.1$G against $36.1$G) and cuts the T4 latency by $19\%$ ($9.3$~ms against $11.6$~ms), for a loss of at most $1.0$ point on the primary cohorts. Where accuracy matters more than latency, the fg/bg decoder with PASSE is the better choice. Because these variants were compared on the development cohorts, this choice is itself part of the adaptive design discussed in Section~\ref{sec:limits}.

Table~\ref{tab:eff} lists the cost of each model, and Figure~\ref{fig:latency} plots accuracy against latency. DANG has the fewest total and trained parameters of all compared models, but about twice the MACs per frame of the Res2Net and PVTv2 models ($25.1$G against $10.8$--$13.0$G), because the frozen encoder runs at $448\times448$. With FP16 weights in a CUDA graph its batch-1 latency ($9.3$~ms, about $107$ forward passes per second on the device) is below that of Polyp-PVT ($10.1$~ms) and PraNet-V2 ($10.2$~ms) and above that of PraNet ($8.4$~ms); the end-to-end time of a clinical pipeline would add transfer and post-processing. This advantage depends on CUDA graphs: with FP16 weights alone, Polyp-PVT ($18.3$~ms) is faster than DANG ($20.7$~ms). FP16 weights do not change DANG's accuracy: in the training runs, the FP16 copy of every seed scores within $0.02$ points of the FP32 model on the three primary cohorts. SegDINO, at its $256\times256$ input and with a light head, is the fastest model ($3.7$~ms, $6.9$G MACs), but far less accurate. In eager mode DANG has the lowest batch-1 latency of the $352\times352$ models ($22.7$~ms) but the lowest batch-$8$ throughput ($41$ against $155$--$174$ images per second), because its encoder stays in FP32 there; batched offline processing would need the FP16 encoder. Training DANG takes $27$ minutes per seed on one T4, against $66$ and $203$ minutes for PraNet and PraNet-V2 on the same GPU.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Development on the test cohorts.} Following the standard benchmark, which has no validation split, DANG's design, including the choice of decoder, was developed while inspecting the test cohorts. Results on Kvasir, ClinicDB, ColonDB, ETIS, CVC-300 and PolypGen are therefore development results, and their tests do not account for this selection. PolypDB was never used for design and was evaluated once, on the final model; it is the confirmatory result, and there DANG leads every retrained model, by $3.1$ to $17.4$ points.
  \item \textbf{Dependent frames.} The cohorts consist of video frames, and patient or sequence identifiers are not available for all of them, so image-level tests are descriptive; our inference rests on five training seeds, which gives only four degrees of freedom.
  \item \textbf{Boundary precision.} DANG's boundary F1 is below that of Polyp-PVT on three of the four external cohorts, and it trails Polyp-PVT on the in-domain ClinicDB.
  \item \textbf{Recipes differ.} The compared models use the recipes of their papers, DANG its own; in particular only DANG trains with Fourier amplitude mixing and mixed precision. The comparison is between methods as published, as is usual on this benchmark; isolating the contribution of each recipe element under matched training budgets is left to future work.
  \item \textbf{Hardware.} DANG and most compared models were trained on NVIDIA T4 GPUs; Polyp-PVT, whose $99$-epoch schedule exceeds our T4 session limit, was trained on cloud GPUs of another type.
  \item \textbf{One training split.} All models are trained on the same two centres; we do not test other training sources or label budgets.
  \item \textbf{Scope.} We evaluate single frames, not video, and report no clinical reader study.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}
DANG segments polyps from a frozen DINOv3 ViT-S/16 with convolutional bottleneck adapters, a token pyramid, a scale-aware decoder and a dual-prototype margin head, training $1.9$M of $23.5$M parameters. On the held-out PolypDB, evaluated once, it reaches $89.8\%$ mean Dice, $3.1$ points above the strongest retrained model. On the development cohorts it exceeds every compared model on ETIS-LaribPolypDB ($+7.3$ points) and PolypGen ($+2.7$ points), shows no significant difference to Polyp-PVT on CVC-ColonDB, and trails Polyp-PVT on the in-domain CVC-ClinicDB and in boundary F1; its gains come mainly from fewer failed frames. The adapters are essential ($5.5$--$10.8$ points on the primary cohorts), the prototype head adds a small $0.2$--$1.0$ points that are not significant across seeds, and a heavier fg/bg decoder with a support envelope is up to $1$ point more accurate while DANG's decoder is $19\%$ faster ($9.3$~ms per frame on a T4 with CUDA graphs). Next steps are a validation split for design choices, training on other centres, sequence-level statistics, video-level evaluation and a reader study.

\section{Implementation Details}
\label{app:impl}

\begin{table*}[!t]
  \centering
  \caption{\textbf{DANG hyperparameters.} Lesion area $a$ is the ground-truth foreground percentage of the image.}
  \label{tab:impl}
  \footnotesize
  \setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
  \begin{tabular}{@{}l p{0.8\textwidth}@{}}
    \toprule
    \textbf{Item} & \textbf{Setting} \\
    \midrule
    Encoder & DINOv3 ViT-S/16 (LVD-1689M), frozen, input $448\times448$ (resized from $352\times352$), run in FP32 during training (its attention logits overflow FP16 under autocast); FP16 weights at inference change Dice by at most $0.02$ points \\
    Adapters & residual convolutional bottleneck (Eq.~\eqref{eq:convlora}), rank $16$, after each of the $12$ blocks; readout after blocks $3$, $6$, $9$, $12$; $192$ decoder channels \\
    Optimiser & AdamW; learning rate $10^{-3}$ (adapters), $4\times10^{-4}$ (all other trained modules) \\
    Weight decay & $10^{-4}$; none on adapters, normalisation, bias, gain and prototype parameters \\
    Schedule & linear warm-up for $2$ epochs, then cosine decay to $5\%$; $20$ epochs; batch size $16$ \\
    Weight averaging & EMA with decay $\min(0.992,\,(1+t)/(10+t))$ at step $t$; final EMA weights are evaluated \\
    Other & gradient-norm clipping at $3.0$; FP16 mixed precision on T4 \\
    Augmentation & scale $0.65$--$0.90$ ($p=0.3$) or $0.95$--$1.20$ with crop or pad; horizontal and vertical flips ($p=0.5$ each); rotation by $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ or $270^\circ$ ($p=0.5$); brightness, contrast, saturation $\pm15\%$ ($p=0.4$); hue $\pm0.04$ ($p=0.3$); gamma $0.8$--$1.25$ ($p=0.3$); Fourier amplitude mix with a random batch partner, $\lambda\sim U(0,1)$ ($p=0.5$) \\
    \midrule
    Image weight & $w=\mathrm{clip}\bigl((3/(a+0.35))^{0.4},\,1,\,2.4\bigr)$, normalised to mean $1$ in the batch \\
    BCE+Dice & $0.5$ binary cross-entropy (pixel mean) $+\,0.5\,(1-\text{soft Dice})$, Dice smoothing $1$ \\
    Tversky & false-positive weight $0.45+0.15\,\sigma((a-1.5)/0.5)$, false-negative weight $1$ minus it, smoothing $1$ \\
    Far-field loss & mean over all pixels of $\sigma(Z)\cdot\tfrac14\sum_{r}\mathbb{1}[\text{outside the mask dilated by } r]$, $r\in\{4,8,14,20\}$ pixels; not image-weighted \\
    Prototype head & $K=8+8$ prototypes, dimension $128$; $\beta=6$; $\tau$ learned, initialised at $12$ and clamped to $[4,25]$ \\
    & $w_{\text{a}}=10\cdot\tfrac12\tanh(\theta_{\text{a}})$, $w_{\text{ss}}=8\cdot\tfrac12\tanh(\theta_{\text{ss}})$ with learned $\theta$ \\
    Anchors & momentum $0.95$; foreground where pooled mask $\ge0.35$, background where $\le0.10$; initialised to the normalised prototype means \\
    Self-support & weights $q^2+10^{-4}$ and $(1-q)^2+10^{-4}$, $q$ from a stop-gradient copy of $\pi_{\text{prior}}$ \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table*}

\section*{Data and Code Availability}
All experiments use public, de-identified datasets (Kvasir-SEG~\cite{jha2020kvasir}, CVC-ClinicDB, CVC-ColonDB~\cite{tajbakhsh2015automated}, ETIS-LaribPolypDB~\cite{silva2014toward}, CVC-300, PolypGen~\cite{ali2023polypgen} and PolypDB~\cite{jha2024polypdb}) under their research licences; no new patient data were collected. Code, deduplication manifests, per-image evaluation logs and the scripts that regenerate every table from the raw logs will be released.

is currently pursuing a B.S. degree in Artificial Intelligence at FPT University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. His research interests include computer vision, machine learning, data-driven modeling, and AI for scientific discovery. He is particularly interested in developing innovative AI methodologies to address real-world challenges and advance scientific research. He aspires to pursue a Ph.D. degree and contribute to the advancement of these fields.
\end{IEEEbiographynophoto}

\begin{IEEEbiographynophoto}{Phu-Nguyen Le}
received the B.S. degree in electrical engineering from Da Nang University of Science and Technology, Vietnam, in 2012, and the Ph.D. degree from the University of Ulsan, South Korea, in 2021.
